meta.drug: omega-3 fatty acid ethyl esters (Omacor-type fish oil), 1 g capsule daily = 840 mg marine n-3 fatty acids (460 mg EPA + 380 mg DHA), versus olive-oil placebo. THIS CASE IS ONLY THE OMEGA-3 ARM of the ASCEND 2x2 factorial trial; the aspirin 100 mg vs placebo comparison is a separate question and is not part of this case.
meta.sponsor: University of Oxford (Clinical Trial Service Unit, Nuffield Department of Population Health); funded by the British Heart Foundation; capsules from Mylan (formerly Solvay and Abbott)
meta.mechanism: OMEGA-3 ARM ONLY: low-dose marine omega-3 fatty acid supplementation (EPA + DHA ethyl esters, 1 g/day) intended to raise tissue omega-3 levels (red-cell Omega-3 Index rose 32.5% relative to placebo, S1) and thereby to lower vascular risk through hypothesised triglyceride-lowering, antiarrhythmic, antithrombotic and anti-inflammatory effects. No single molecular target. At 1 g/day the lipid effect is small (ORIGIN, same dose: triglycerides -14.5 mg/dL vs placebo, S8; ASCEND subset: non-HDL-C -2.4 mg/dL and apoB -1.2 mg/dL, both not significant, S4); triglycerides were not measured in ASCEND. Pharmacological triglyceride lowering needs >3 g/day (S12). target_symbol LPL is used, as in the STRENGTH and REDUCE-IT cases, only as the human-genetic proxy for the triglyceride-lowering pathway (Ference 2019, S13), not as a confirmed drug target.
meta.modality: dietary supplement / small molecule (oral fish-oil capsule, 1 g once daily; mailed to participants)
meta.indication: primary prevention of serious vascular events in adults aged >=40 years with diabetes (any type, 94% type 2) and no evidence of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (UK)

n_randomized.quote: From June 2005 through July 2011, a total of 15,480 patients underwent randomization.
n_randomized.note: 7740 omega-3 and 7740 placebo (Fig. 1). 2x2 factorial: each omega-3 group split 3870/3870 by aspirin vs placebo aspirin. Interaction with aspirin assignment P = 0.71 (S1).

median_followup.quote: At a mean follow-up of 7.4 years, data were available for 57,022 person-years in the fatty acid group and 56,924 person-years in the placebo group.
median_followup.note: Median not reported; mean 7.4 years. Complete follow-up for 99.1%. Mean adherence 77% omega-3 vs 76% placebo ('The mean adherence to the assigned regimen (weighted according to person-years at risk) was 77% in the fatty acid group and 76% in the placebo group.').

primary_endpoint.value: First serious vascular event: nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke (excluding confirmed intracranial hemorrhage) or TIA, or vascular death excluding intracranial hemorrhage. Secondary: serious vascular event or any arterial revascularization.
primary_endpoint.quote: Thus, the prespecified primary efficacy outcome was the first serious vascular event, which was defined as a composite of nonfatal myocardial infarction or stroke (excluding confirmed intracranial hemorrhage), TIA, or vascular death excluding intracranial hemorrhage.
primary_endpoint.note: Endpoint changed during recruitment: 'While recruitment was still ongoing, we modified the original primary outcome to include transient ischemic attack (TIA) in the definition of serious vascular events, a change that was made to increase the statistical power of the trial.' (S1). Supplement S4: the 2003 design assumed 2%/year for the original composite but the blinded rate was 'at around 0.6% per year'; the protocol amendment (approved early 2011) added TIA, raised n to >=15,000 and follow-up to >=7 years.

inclusion_key_criteria.value: Age >=40 years (no upper limit); diabetes mellitus of any type; no evidence of cardiovascular disease; no clear indication or contraindication for n-3 fatty acids or aspirin; over-the-counter fish oil allowed only if <1 g/day; mail-based recruitment with 8-10 week placebo run-in
inclusion_key_criteria.quote: Men and women who were at least 40 years of age (without an upper age limit) were considered eligible if they had received a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus (any type) but did not have evidence of cardiovascular disease.
inclusion_key_criteria.note: Registry S3: 'Aged ≥ 40 years.' and 'No previous history of vascular disease.' Fish-oil users had to stop or keep the dose below 1 g ('provided that the daily dose was less than 1 g'). 10% reported over-the-counter fish oil at baseline and 7% at 6.7 years, no difference between groups (S1).

planned_events.unit: serious vascular events (both groups combined, expected)
planned_events.quote: The expected 1300 incident vascular events will approximately double the information currently available about the effects of using aspirin for primary prevention in people with diabetes.
planned_events.location: Methods, Sample size and predicted number of events
planned_events.note: Pre-readout design paper (Am Heart J, online 2017-12-24). The sentence concerns the aspirin question but the expected count is for the trial-wide serious vascular event outcome shared by both factorial comparisons. Observed for the omega-3 comparison: 689 + 712 = 1401 (S1). NEJM S1 gives no explicit event target.

assumed_rrr.quote: On the basis of a rate of serious vascular events of 1.2 to 1.3% per year, as observed in both groups combined after recruitment was complete, we determined that 7.5 years of scheduled treatment and follow-up would provide a power of 90% at an alpha value of less than 0.05 to detect a relative between-group difference of 15%.
assumed_rrr.note: Supplement S4: '90% power at p<0.05 to detect a 15% difference in the risk of SVE in the aspirin group compared to the placebo group, with similar power for the omega-3 FA comparison.' Pre-readout S6 states the same (>90% at 2P<.05, 15%, 7.5 years). Original 2003 design: 20-25% reduction with 10,000 patients over 5 years (S4).

power.quote: 7.5 years of scheduled treatment and follow-up would provide a power of 90% at an alpha value of less than 0.05 to detect a relative between-group difference of 15%.

alpha.quote: A two-tailed P value of less than 0.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance for the primary efficacy outcome.

stopped_early.quote: During a mean follow-up of 7.4 years (adherence rate, 76%), a serious vascular event occurred in 689 patients (8.9%) in the fatty acid group and in 712 (9.2%) in the placebo group
stopped_early.note: Ran to the scheduled end of treatment (registry primary completion 2018-03-12, S3); not stopped early. Note the mid-trial endpoint and sample-size amendment (see primary_endpoint).

baseline.note: non-HDL-C. Measured in about 64% with a usable baseline sample. Background statin use 74.8% omega-3 vs 75.7% placebo (S1 Table 1: 'Statin 5791 (74.8) 5862 (75.7)'). 112 mg/dL = 2.90 mmol/L (x0.02586). Labelled biomarker 'non-HDL-C'.
HDL-C. Total cholesterol mean 161 mg/dL in both groups.

NOT MEASURED: triglycerides (S4: 'Triglyceride levels were not measured as, in earlier studies, these had not been found to be sufficiently stable in mailed blood samples, although later data refuted this.'). LDL-C also not reported.
SBP, measured when the blood sample was taken; unknown in 28.7%.

Exploratory vascular death 186 vs 228, 0.81 (0.67-0.99) (Fig. 3). No trend over time: by year <3 1.01, 3-<5 0.97, 5-<7 0.91, >=7 0.98; trend P=0.64 (Fig. 2B).

genetics.finding: Rare APOC3 loss-of-function mutations lower triglycerides by 39% and are associated with reduced CHD risk, supporting causality of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins.
genetics.effect: OR 0.60 (0.47-0.75) for CHD in carriers; TG 39% lower
genetics.quote: The risk of coronary heart disease among 498 carriers of any rare APOC3 mutation was 40% lower than the risk among 110,472 noncarriers (odds ratio, 0.60; 95% confidence interval, 0.47 to 0.75; P=4×10(-6)).
genetics.note: PRE-readout. Abstract read via Europe PMC. Large lifelong TG lowering, far beyond the TG effect of 1 g/day omega-3 (ORIGIN -14.5 mg/dL, S8).

genetics.finding: Mendelian randomization: triglyceride-lowering LPL variants and LDL-C-lowering LDLR variants give the same CHD protection per 10 mg/dL lower apoB; triglycerides have no independent association after adjusting for apoB, so benefit of TG lowering is proportional to the absolute apoB change.
genetics.effect: OR 0.771 (0.741-0.802) per 10 mg/dL lower apoB via LPL score; TG adjusted for apoB OR 1.014 (0.965-1.065)
genetics.quote: Triglyceride-lowering LPL variants and LDL-C-lowering LDLR variants were associated with similar lower risk of CHD per unit difference in ApoB. Therefore, the clinical benefit of lowering triglyceride and LDL-C levels may be proportional to the absolute change in ApoB.
genetics.note: POST-readout (JAMA online 2019-01-29; Europe PMC lists 2019-01-01). Abstract read. ASCEND apoB difference was -1.2 mg/dL (95% CI -3.2 to 0.8) in a subset (S4), which under this model predicts almost no benefit.

genetics.finding: Mendelian randomization of circulating omega-3 PUFA (UK Biobank GWAS, n=114,999): genetically higher DHA and total omega-3 were not protective; nominal harmful associations attenuated after accounting for LDL-C or excluding the FADS locus.
genetics.effect: no protective effect of genetically higher circulating omega-3 on CVD
genetics.quote: Overall, our Mendelian randomization findings do not support a protective role of circulating PUFA concentration on the risk of CVDs.
genetics.note: POST-readout. Abstract read (PMC9190170 open). Authors caution 'horizontal pleiotropy via lipoprotein-related traits could be a key source of bias'. Omega-3 fatty acids have no single protein target; circulating omega-3 level is the closest genetic proxy for the supplement's direct effect.

genetics.finding: Mendelian randomization (UK Biobank allele scores and CARDIoGRAMplusC4D): higher genetically predicted EPA levels associated with lower CAD risk.
genetics.effect: EPA: lower CAD risk (direction only, abstract gives no estimate)
genetics.quote: Higher genetically predicted eicosapentaenoic acid and dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid levels were significantly associated with a lower risk of CAD both in the allele-score-based and summary-level MR analyses.
genetics.note: POST-readout. Abstract read. Contradicts S14 in direction for EPA: genetic evidence on omega-3 levels is mixed, so target genetics is 'uncertain'.

consensus_explanation.summary: Experts read the ASCEND omega-3 comparison as a large, long, well-conducted and truly neutral trial (15,480 patients, 7.4 years, 1401 events, rate ratio 0.97, 0.87-1.08). The investigators concluded that 1 g/day fish oil gives little or no benefit, in line with the 2018 meta-analysis of 10 earlier trials (major vascular events RR 0.97), and that routine supplementation is not supported. The leading expert explanation is the dose: 1 g/day (840 mg EPA+DHA) barely changes atherogenic lipids (ASCEND subset non-HDL-C -2.4 mg/dL and apoB -1.2 mg/dL, both not significant; triglycerides not measured; about -14.5 mg/dL triglycerides at the same dose in ORIGIN), while pharmacological triglyceride lowering needs more than 3 g/day; the authors themselves noted that higher doses (2-4 g) lower triglycerides. The REDUCE-IT investigators said it is not known whether the lack of benefit in earlier trials was due to the low dose or the low EPA:DHA ratio, and the 2019 updated meta-analysis found benefit rising linearly with dose and suggested that a high dose may be needed. Under the apoB model (Ference 2019) the tiny apoB change predicts essentially no benefit, so the trial could not have shown one even with 90% power for a 15% reduction. As a secondary reason, supplementation raised the red-cell Omega-3 Index by 32.5% versus placebo without any benefit, and Mendelian randomization of circulating omega-3 levels is null or mixed, which argues against a large non-lipid effect of omega-3 status itself at this dose.
consensus_explanation.review_note: Primary effect_too_small because the drug's quantifiable mechanism (triglyceride-rich lipoprotein / apoB lowering) is causal but was moved by a trivial amount at 1 g/day. biomarker_not_causal is secondary: the intended biomarker of omega-3 status rose as planned without benefit and genetics on omega-3 levels does not show clear protection; this is debated (S15 finds EPA protective).

open_questions: Triglycerides were not measured in ASCEND (mailed samples were thought unstable), so the trial's own triglyceride effect is unknown; the TG change at the same dose comes from ORIGIN (S8). Calculator inputs therefore use the subset non-HDL-C and apoB differences.

Lipid differences (S4 Table S7) come from a random subset of about 471-620 patients per group at a mean of 2.5 years, and LDL-C was not reported; percent changes in the calc file are DERIVED (difference / subset baseline).
Expected effect by CTT-type conversion (DERIVED, not from a source): non-HDL-C -0.062 mmol/L gives 0.78^0.062 = 0.985, i.e. about 1.5% relative reduction, far below the 15% the trial was powered for.

Exploratory vascular death reduction (186 vs 228; rate ratio 0.81, 0.67-0.99) was not adjusted for multiplicity; the 2019 meta-analysis (S11) reads it as support for a modest benefit while the ASCEND authors did not.

Whether higher-dose or EPA-only formulations would work in this population is not answered by ASCEND: REDUCE-IT (4 g EPA, mineral-oil placebo) was positive while STRENGTH (4 g EPA+DHA, corn-oil placebo) was neutral.
